title: 367 - Maniac Mansion
method: claude-code: written from the transcript, links verified by script

items.name: Maniac Mansion
items.description: The episode's game: Lucasfilm's point-and-click adventure, ported from computers to the NES, where teens storm a mad scientist's mansion.

items.name: Lucasfilm Games
items.description: The studio behind Maniac Mansion, whose later games reuse the gas can joke.

items.name: Day of the Tentacle
items.description: The 1993 sequel to Maniac Mansion, widely respected as a classic adventure game.

items.name: Sierra On-Line
items.description: Publisher of other point-and-click adventures, some known for illogical puzzles.

items.name: Commodore 64
items.description: One of the home computers where Maniac Mansion first appeared.

items.name: Apple II
items.description: Another home computer where the original Maniac Mansion appeared.

items.name: Ron Gilbert
items.description: Co-creator of Maniac Mansion, credited with coining the word cutscene.

items.name: SCUMM
items.description: The Script Creation Utility for Maniac Mansion, the custom engine with the verb-and-noun interface.

items.name: Shadowgate
items.description: Earlier NES adventure game on the Essential Games List, compared and contrasted with Maniac Mansion.

items.name: Zork
items.description: Text adventure where you type commands, contrasted with clicking verbs.

items.name: The Rocky Horror Picture Show
items.description: Cult musical film whose logo and mad-scientist vibe the hosts see in the game.

links.label: Wikipedia: The Rocky Horror Picture Show
links.note: 1975 musical comedy horror film by Jim Sharman

items.name: A Nightmare on Elm Street
items.description: Slasher film the developers reportedly drew on for tone.

links.label: Wikipedia: A Nightmare on Elm Street

items.name: Friday the 13th
items.description: Slasher film series cited as another inspiration for the game's teen-horror setup.

items.name: Wes Craven
items.description: Director of A Nightmare on Elm Street, whose film the hosts call campy.

items.name: Scary Movie
items.description: Horror parody film used to describe the game's slapstick tone.

items.name: Sweet Home
items.description: Horror game the hosts covered on their other podcast, a more straight horror contrast.

items.name: Nintendo
items.description: The company that required censorship of Maniac Mansion, though it missed the microwave hamster.

items.name: Nintendo Power
items.description: The magazine that put Maniac Mansion on its cover and offered a $7.95 hint book.

links.label: Wikipedia: Nintendo Power
links.note: American video game magazine and podcast (1988–2012)

items.name: Maniac Mansion (TV series)
items.description: The 1990 comedy series based on the game, which ran three seasons.

items.name: Eugene Levy
items.description: Actor and comedy figure involved in the Maniac Mansion TV show.

items.name: Twin Peaks
items.description: Surreal 1990 TV series compared to the Maniac Mansion show's meta tone.

items.name: Back to the Future
items.description: Film joked about for the idea of having a TV in every room.

items.name: ZX Spectrum
items.description: British home computer mentioned when asking how many people had gaming computers.

items.name: Windows 95
items.description: The operating system that finally gave one host a computer able to play games.

items.name: Game Boy
items.description: Nintendo handheld the Famicom version's art looks similar to.

items.name: Super Nintendo Entertainment System
items.description: Console whose games reportedly sold for as much as $80.

items.name: Nintendo 64
items.description: Console whose games were around $50 and later got pricier.

items.name: PlayStation
items.description: Console whose games were typically $50 in the hosts' memory.

links.label: Wikipedia: PlayStation (console)
links.note: Home video game console by Sony

items.name: PlayStation 3
items.description: Console era when game prices rose to $60.

links.label: Wikipedia: PlayStation 3
links.note: Home video game console by Sony

items.name: Grand Theft Auto VI
items.description: Upcoming Rockstar game used in a debate about $100 games.

items.name: Red Dead Redemption 2
items.description: Rockstar game one host would pay $100 for.

items.name: Rockstar Games
items.description: Publisher whose scale of games might justify higher prices.

items.name: Assassin's Creed
items.description: Series used as an example of games not worth $100.

items.name: Cutscene
items.description: Term credited to Ron Gilbert's Maniac Mansion, whose manual explains what a cutscene is.

links.label: Wikipedia: Cutscene
links.note: Sequence in a video game that is not interactive, breaking up the gameplay

items.name: Tommy Pickles
items.description: The baby leader of the Rugrats, compared to Dave as the group's leader.

links.label: Wikipedia: Tommy Pickles
links.note: Fictional character in the Rugrats franchise

items.name: Myst
items.description: Adventure game one host could not stand playing on a PlayStation controller.

items.name: Mission: Impossible
items.description: Next week's NES game.

items.name: NEStalgia Essential Games List
items.description: The show's running vote on which NES games are essential.
